notes.cubit: The common cubit, the length of the forearm from elbow to fingertip. It is usually taken as about 45 cm (estimates run from about 44 to 52 cm) and was divided into 2 spans, 6 handbreadths or 24 fingers.
notes.cubit.long: A longer cubit, a common cubit plus a handbreadth: 7 handbreadths instead of 6 (Ezek 40:5). About 52 cm (roughly 50–53 cm); it is used in Ezekiel's temple vision and is probably the cubit "after the first measure" of 2 Chr 3:3.
notes.span: The spread hand from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger: half a cubit, or 3 handbreadths. About 23 cm with the common cubit.
notes.handbreadth: The width of the four fingers at their base: a sixth of a cubit, or 4 fingers. About 7.5 cm with the common cubit.
notes.finger: The width of a finger, the smallest Hebrew length: a quarter of a handbreadth and a twenty-fourth of a cubit, about 1.9 cm.
notes.reed: A measuring reed or rod. Ezekiel's reed was 6 long cubits (Ezek 40:5), about 3.1 m. Where its length is not stated, as in Revelation, the same length is assumed.
notes.furlong: The Greek stadion, the length of a race course: 600 Greek feet, an eighth of a Roman mile. Local standards ranged from about 177 to 192 m; about 185 m is usual.
notes.mile: The Roman mile, a thousand double paces (5,000 Roman feet), about 1.48 km. It equalled 8 stadia (furlongs).
notes.fathom: The Greek orgyia, the reach of a man's outstretched arms, used in sounding the depth of the sea (Acts 27:28). About 1.85 m; 100 fathoms made a stadion.
notes.sabbath.journey: The distance Jewish tradition allowed a person to walk on the Sabbath, reckoned as 2,000 cubits (compare Josh 3:4). Roughly 0.9–1 km, depending on the cubit used.
notes.acre: The Hebrew tsemed, literally a "yoke": the land a pair of oxen could plough in a day. Its size is uncertain; estimates of roughly 2,500 to 4,500 m² are common, and about 0.4 hectare is used here.
notes.homer: The largest Hebrew dry measure, literally a "donkey-load". It held 10 ephahs (Ezek 45:11), about 220 L if the ephah is about 22 L; older estimates are nearly twice that.
notes.cor: A large measure equal to the homer: 10 ephahs, or 10 baths for liquids (Ezek 45:14). About 220 L on the smaller estimate of the ephah, up to about 400 L on older ones.
notes.ephah: The standard Hebrew dry measure, equal in volume to the liquid bath (Ezek 45:11). It is usually estimated at about 22 L, though older estimates run as high as 36–40 L; it held 3 seahs or 10 omers.
notes.seah: A dry measure, a third of an ephah, rendered "measure" in the KJV. About 7.3 L on the usual estimate of the ephah; it held 6 cabs.
notes.omer: A dry measure, "the tenth part of an ephah" (Exod 16:36), the daily portion of manna for one person. About 2.2 L on the usual estimate of the ephah.
notes.cab: A small dry measure, a sixth of a seah and an eighteenth of an ephah (later Jewish sources: 4 logs). About 1.2 L on the usual estimate of the ephah.
notes.issaron: The KJV "tenth deal" is a tenth part of an ephah, the same quantity as the omer, used for flour in the offerings. About 2.2 L on the usual estimate of the ephah.
notes.choinix: The Greek choenix, a dry measure of about 1.1 L, roughly one person's daily ration of grain. In Rev 6:6 a choenix of wheat costs a denarius, a whole day's wage: a famine price.
notes.saton: The Greek form of the Hebrew seah, a third of an ephah. About 7.3 L on the usual estimate of the ephah; Josephus' equivalent implies about 13 L.
notes.koros: The Greek form of the Hebrew cor, equal to 10 ephahs or 10 baths. About 220 L on the usual estimate; Josephus' equivalent implies nearly 400 L.
notes.bath: The standard Hebrew liquid measure, equal in volume to the ephah (Ezek 45:11). Inscribed storage jars suggest about 22 L; older estimates run to 36–40 L. It held 6 hins.
notes.hin: A liquid measure, a sixth of a bath, used for the oil and wine of the offerings. About 3.7 L on the usual estimate of the bath; it held 12 logs.
notes.log: The smallest Hebrew liquid measure, used for oil (Lev 14), a seventy-second of a bath. About 0.3 L on the usual estimate of the bath.
notes.metretes: The Greek metretes ("measurer"), a liquid measure of about 39 L on the Attic standard. Each stone jar at Cana (John 2:6) held 2 or 3 of them, roughly 80–120 L.
notes.talent: The largest Hebrew weight, 3,000 shekels (Exod 38:25–26) or 60 minas. About 34 kg with a shekel of about 11.4 g; estimates range from about 30 to 41 kg.
notes.mina: A weight of 50 shekels, about 570 g with a shekel of about 11.4 g. Ezekiel's mina (Ezek 45:12) is 60 shekels; 60 minas made a talent.
notes.shekel: The basic Hebrew weight, used to weigh out silver before there were coins. About 11.4 g; excavated weights range roughly from 10 to 13 g. It was 2 bekahs or 20 gerahs (Exod 30:13).
notes.bekah: Half a shekel (Exod 38:26), the sum each man counted in the census gave for the sanctuary. About 5.7 g; inscribed bekah weights have been excavated.
notes.gerah: The smallest Hebrew weight, a twentieth of a shekel (Exod 30:13), about 0.57 g. The word probably means a grain or bean.
notes.litra: The Roman pound (Latin libra, Greek litra) of 12 ounces, about 327 g. It is the "pound" of ointment in John 12:3 and of spices in John 19:39.
notes.denarius: The Roman silver coin and a labourer's ordinary pay for a day (Matt 20:2), so it is the baseline here: 1 denarius = 1 day's wages. In the 1st century it held about 3.8 g of silver; 16 assaria made a denarius.
notes.drachma: The Greek silver coin, treated in New Testament times as equal in value to the denarius, about a day's wage. The Attic drachma weighed about 4.3 g of silver; later and local issues were lighter.
notes.didrachma: A two-drachma piece, the sum of the yearly half-shekel tax for the Temple (Matt 17:24; Exod 30:13). Worth about 2 days' wages.
notes.stater: A silver coin worth 4 drachmas (a tetradrachm), probably the Tyrian shekel of about 14 g. Peter's stater (Matt 17:27) paid the Temple tax for two; about 4 days' wages.
notes.assarion: A small Roman bronze coin (the as), a sixteenth of a denarius; two sparrows sold for one (Matt 10:29). About three-quarters of an hour of a day's wages.
notes.quadrans: The smallest Roman coin, a quarter of an assarion and a sixty-fourth of a denarius. Two lepta made one (Mark 12:42).
notes.lepton: The smallest coin in use in Judea, a tiny bronze piece worth half a quadrans, a hundred-and-twenty-eighth of a denarius. The widow gave two (Mark 12:42).
notes.mina.money: A sum of 100 drachmas, about 100 days' wages (Luke 19:13). It was a unit of account, not a coin; 60 minas made a talent.
notes.talent.money: A sum of 6,000 drachmas or denarii: about 6,000 days' wages, some twenty years of a labourer's work. It was a unit of account, about 26 kg of silver on the Attic standard.
notes.daric: A Persian gold coin of about 8.4 g, first struck under Darius I, rendered "dram" in the KJV. Its value in wages is uncertain; Xenophon reports mercenaries paid a daric a month, roughly 25 days' wages. Some scholars take the word in Ezra and Nehemiah as the Greek drachma instead.
notes.silver.piece: "Pieces of silver" does not name the coin. Judas' thirty (Matt 26:15) were probably Tyrian shekels (tetradrachms) of about 14 g, each about 4 days' wages; if denarii were meant, each was a day's wage.
notes.hour.1: The first hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 7 a.m.. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.2: The second hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 8 a.m.. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.3: The third hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 9 a.m.. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.4: The fourth hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 10 a.m.. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.5: The fifth hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 11 a.m.. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.6: The sixth hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about noon. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.7: The seventh hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 1 p.m.. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.8: The eighth hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 2 p.m.. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.9: The ninth hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 3 p.m.. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.10: The tenth hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 4 p.m.. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.11: The eleventh hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 5 p.m.. The daylight was divided into 12 hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
notes.hour.12: The twelfth hour of the day by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise (about 6 a.m.): about 6 p.m.. It closed the day at about sunset.
notes.watch.hebrew.1: The first of the three night watches of the Old Testament ("the beginning of the watches", Lam 2:19), from sunset to about 10 p.m.
notes.watch.hebrew.2: The middle of the three Old Testament night watches (Judg 7:19), from about 10 p.m. to about 2 a.m.
notes.watch.hebrew.3: The last of the three Old Testament night watches (Exod 14:24; 1 Sam 11:11), from about 2 a.m. to sunrise.
notes.watch.roman.1: The first of the four Roman night watches used in the New Testament, from about 6 p.m. to 9 p.m.. Mark 13:35 calls it "even".
notes.watch.roman.2: The second of the four Roman night watches used in the New Testament, from about 9 p.m. to midnight. Mark 13:35 calls it "midnight".
notes.watch.roman.3: The third of the four Roman night watches used in the New Testament, from about midnight to 3 a.m.. Mark 13:35 calls it "cockcrowing".
notes.watch.roman.4: The fourth of the four Roman night watches used in the New Testament, from about 3 a.m. to 6 a.m.. Mark 13:35 calls it "morning".
